*hier*de{}|Alternative forms}hie hie und da|Etymology}From Middle High German hier,from Old High German hier,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hēr. Cognate with from Dutch hier,from English here,from Swedish här.}The predominant form in Middle High German and throughout modern dialects of High German is from Middle High German hie (and variants) with loss of the final ''-r''. The form  begins to gain ground from the late 16th century (in spite of Luther’s usage),which may point to influence by cognate from Middle Low German hīr,from Middle Low German hēr (where no ''r-''less form seems to exist; but compare modern from Limburgish heej).|Pronunciation}IPA:hi(ː)ɐ̯}Ⓓb/b1/De-hier.ogg}Ⓓb/b7/De-hier2.ogg}De-at-hier.ogg(Austria)}Rhymes:iːɐ̯|Adverb}#location here; in this place; refers to an environment one is currently in,or to something within reach}•Ich bin '''hier''' in diesem Dorf geboren.}•I was born '''here''' in this village.}•Setzen wir uns '''hier''' aufs Sofa.}•Let’s sit down '''here''' on the sofa.}#location there; right there; in that place; refers to something that is considered nearby,or can be seen and pointed at}•synononym da}•Die Kirche ist gleich '''hier''' am Ende der Straße.}•The church is right '''there''' at the end of the street.}•Siehst du die Wolke '''hier''' neben der Bergspitze?}•Can you see that cloud '''there''' next to the mountain top?}#abstract here gloss:within this context}•Die Frist wurde '''hier''' überhaupt nicht erwähnt.}•The deadline was not mentioned '''here''' at all.}#used with the definite article or the determiner l+de+dieser++this,that to express proximity (“this”)}•Die Kneipe '''hier''' ist sehr beliebt.}•'''This''' pub is very popular.}•'''Hier''' der Stuhl ist kaputt.}•'''This''' chair is broken.}•Dieser Schrank '''hier''' ist 200 Jahre alt.}•'''This''' cupboard is 200 years old.|Derived terms}hieran}hierauf}hieraus}hierbei}hierbleiben}hier drin}hier drüben}hierdurch}hierfür}hiergegen}hierher}hierhin}hiermit}hiernach}hiervon|See also}da}dort}her}hier und da}hiesig|Interjection}hier:}#colloquial Used for emphasis or to call for attention,often when changing the subject}•'''Hier''',der Markus ist doch jetzt auch verheiratet,ne?}•'''Hey,wait''',Markus is married now,too,isn't he?

*hinterer*de{}|Etymology}from Old High German hintaro|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhɪntəʁɐ/}Ⓓ3/3d/De-hinterer.ogg|Adjective}#back,hind}•Dein Mantel ist in dem '''hinteren''' Zimmer.}•Your coat is in the '''back''' room.|Usage notes}Since the adjective is already semantically comparative in its positive form,the grammatical comparative forms are very rare and heard in the vernacular only. They might be used to mean “even further in the back”. For example:''Dein Mantel ist in dem hinteren Zimmer.'' − ''In diesem?'' − ''Nein,in dem noch '''hintereren'''.'' (“Your coat is in the back room.” – “This one?” − “No,the one behind that.”)}The superlative forms are perfectly normal,being the same as cog:hindmost.

*hissen*de{}|Etymology}16th century,from gml,of from German nocap1 origin. Possibly the same word as from Middle Low German hissen,from Middle Low German hitzen,from Middle Dutch hissen (modern from Dutch ophitsen),from Old French hicier,all meaning “to set hounds on”. These can be compared to from Proto-Germanic ⋆hatjaną (whence High German hetzen),but the phonetics are highly problematic. Therefore the group is usually considered from German titleimitative,immediately comparable to from English hiss.}The use for “hoisting” appears first in the mid-15th century in from Middle Dutch hîsen (cf. modern from Dutch hijsen) and in the from Middle English - nautical interjection from Middle English hissa (cf. from Scots heeze,from English hoise,whence from English hoist). The word then quickly spread to other Germanic as well as Romance languages. Such cognates include from Danish hejse,from French hisser,from Spanish izar,from Italian issare.|Pronunciation}IPA:/hɪsən/}Ⓓ6/61/De-hissen.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#transitive to hoist (a flag or sail)

*hoch-*de{}|Etymology}A prefixed variation of the adverb hoch.|Pronunciation}IPA:hoːχ}Ⓓ5/51/De-hoch-.ogg|Prefix}hoch-:}#A prefix,equivalent high or up}•Antonym:nieder-|Derived terms}prefixsee:de
*hoch*de{}|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆kewk-}From Middle High German hōch,from Old High German hōh,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hauh,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hauhaz,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆kewk-,a suffixed form of from Proto-Indo-European ⋆kew-. Compare from Dutch hoog,from English high,from Swedish hög.}The irregular declension from the stem  is due to the development of from Old High German -h-,which in Middle High German became/x/in coda position,but/h/elsewhere (the latter was then gradually lost,starting from the north). Stem alternations of this kind were usually levelled in modern German,as for example in nah (but compare nach),Schuh (from Middle High German nāch,from Middle High German schuoch). Most dialects have also levelled ,but the standard language has preserved the alternation in this isolated case.|Pronunciation}IPA:/hoːx/}Ⓓ8/84/De-hoch.ogg}Ⓓb/b0/De-hoch2.ogg}De-at-hoch.ogg(Austria)|Adjective}#high,tall}#high,great,immense}#grand,important}#colloquial hard to comprehend,confusing}•Dieses Rätsel ist mir zu '''hoch'''.}•This riddle beats me.}•litThis riddle is too '''confusing''' for me.|Synonyms}groß|Antonyms}niedrig}nieder|Derived terms}Dreikäsehoch}Hochachtung}hochachtungsvoll}Hochadel}Hochaltar}Hochbau}Hochdero}hochdeutsch}hochdienen}Hochdieselben}Hochdruck}Hochformat}Hochgebirge}hochgefährlich}Hochhaus}Hochmeister}Hochmut}hochnäsig}Hochofen}Hochrad}Hochschule}Hochstapler}Höchstdero}Höchstdieselben}hochtrabend}Hochverrat}Hochwasser}Hochwild}hochwohlgeboren}Hochzeit}halbhoch}ranghoch}wolkenhoch|Adverb}de-adv:höchsten}#up,upwards}#colloquial northwards}•Wir fahren '''hoch''' an die Küste.}•We'll drive '''up''' to the coast.}#mathematics to the power of}•fünf '''hoch''' vier}•five '''to the power of''' four,(5⁴)

*Hochschule*de{}|Etymology}From [[[hoch]+[Schule]]+[t1high]]+[t2school].|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhoːxˌʃuːlə/}Ⓓa/ad/De-Hochschule.ogg}Hoch+schu+le|Noun}(fem.)}#college; university; graduate school; institute; academy gloss:educational institution for advanced studies,usually academic,but also arts,etc.}•Universität|Usage notes}The difference between Hochschule and Universität is that a Universität is reserved for institutions that confer doctorates,whereas Hochschule is a broader term that includes those universities and colleges,which only confer lesser degrees and have no doctoral programs.}Note that ''Hochschule'' is a false friend and does not mean "high school". There is no equivalent to "high school" in Germany. Germany has a completely different school structure than that of the United States. German students attend Realschule from ages 10 to around age 16. After Realschule,they move on to either Gymnasium (comparable to a "college preparatory school") or move on to a Berufsschule ("vocational school").|Derived terms}Fachhochschule

*hoffen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German hoffen (12th c.),from northern from Old High German ⋆hoffōn,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hopōn. It is uncertain whether the (unattested but probable) Old High German form was inherited or rather borrowed from Old Dutch hopon with implementation of the High German consonantism (which was then still entirely predictable). In fact,some scholars consider that all continental forms go back to from Old English hopian,introduced as a religious term by Anglo-Saxon missionaries. The word was at any rate absent from Upper German,where it only established itself in later Middle High German,gradually displacing the now obsolete from Middle High German gedingen. See from English hope for more.|Pronunciation}IPA:-fɱ̍}Ⓓb/bd/De-hoffen.ogg}Ⓓe/e3/De-hoffen2.ogg}hof+fen|Verb}de-verb}#intransitive to hope hoffen ( with  :auf(acc)for something)}•Ich '''hoffe auf''' eine vollständig}•vollständige Heilung.}•I '''hope for''' a complete cure.|Derived terms}Hoffen,Hoffnung}hoffend,gehofft}Hoffender}hoffentlich}erhoffen

*hom.*de{}|Adjective}#Abbreviation of [homerisch]}#}'''1926–8''',Leumann–Hofmann–Szantyr,''Lateinische Grammatik'' I:''Lateinische Laut- und Formenlehre'' (2nd ed.,1977),<span style"font-variant:small-caps">Formenlehre Nomen</span> II.B,§ 273:1.d,http://books.google.co.uk/books?idig4F_lvsZUYC&pgPA290&lpgPA290&dqhom.&sourcebl&ots22Jf-yMajL&sig_81nS8v31kETPDRy55yvqBR1w3A&hlen&saX&ei7WOFVPPhO8KLyATX2IBo&redir_escy#vonepage&qhom.&ffalse page 290:}#}:Das Hauptzeugnis für gr. lang+grc+-ειος,der aeol. Gebrauch von patronym. lang:-ειος bei ''o''-Stämmen,ist eine Neuerung; dieses lang:-ειος ist als Universalsuffix auch bei Kons.-Stämmen verwendet; und es stammt als ''-ios''-Ableitung von den Namen auf lang:-ης,so lang:-ειος neben lang:-ης in Thessalien,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης als lang:-εις geschrieben) l. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; auf Lesbos patronym. 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,weibl. 621,11 als Name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; das Muster für mask. lang:-γένειος usw. war vermutlich nicht-patronym. fem. lang:-εια ('''hom.''' lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια oder lang:-κλέεια).|The main evidence for Greek lang:-ειος,the Aeolic use of patronymic lang:-ειος with ''o''-stems,is an innovation; this lang:-ειος is used as a universal suffix with consonant stems; and it derives from nouns in lang:-ης as a ''-ios''-derivation,thus lang:-ειος is near lang:-ης in Thessaly,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης written as lang:-εις) vid. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; patronymic on Lesbos 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,fem. 621,11 as the name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; the example for the masculine lang:-γένειος etc. was presumably the non-patronymic fem. lang:-εια ('''Homeric''' lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια or lang:-κλέεια).

The plural Hünde is used to some degree regionally and in colloquial varieties,chiefly in southern and western Germany,Austria and Switzerland. Compare Luxembourgish m:Hond (plural:m:Hënn).}By analogy with the plural,the diminutive is sometimes formed without umlaut,yielding Hundchen and Hundlein. *ihr*de{}|Alternative forms}jr|Etymology 1}From Middle High German ir,from Old High German ir,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆jiʀ,from Proto-Germanic ⋆jīz. Cognate with from Low German ji,from Low German jie,from Yiddish איר,from Dutch jij,from Dutch gij,from Dutch je,from Middle Dutch ir,from English ye,from Gothic trjūs.|Pronunciation}qualifier:standard IPA:/iːɐ̯/}Ⓓe/e3/DE-ihr.ogg}Ⓓ0/0b/De-ihr2.ogg}Rhymes:iːɐ̯}qualifier:colloquially in unstressed position IPA:/ɐ/|Pronoun}ihr:}#you,ye plural,familiar|Usage notes}This form is the plural of du,which is used chiefly towards people with whom one is privately acquainted (see there). One uses ''ihr'' towards a group of people if one would address every individual in that group with ''du''. However,the plural ''ihr'' is somewhat less familiar than the singular ''du'',meaning that it can sometimes be used in semi-formal situations where ''du'' towards an individual would not be appropriate. Learners should still,in any case of doubt,use Sie in order to be on the safe side.}The form Ihr (capitalized in writing) was formerly the polite second-person form for both singular and plural (compare French ''vous'' and Early Modern English ''you'') and was used instead of contemporary Sie. Such usage still survives dialectally in some areas,and is encountered in historical contexts (e.g. fiction taking place in the distant past),but is otherwise rarely heard in standard German.}The genitive pronouns are very rare. They are used only in literary and formal style as a genitive object for certain adjectives,prepositions,or verbs which govern the genitive,such as entbehren and gedenken.}In the late 18th century and in the first half of the 19th century,the genitive was also eurer instead of euer,e.g. ''ich erinnere mich eurer'' instead of ''ich erinnere mich euer''.|Etymology 2}From Old High German iru,from Old High German iro.|Pronoun}ihr:}#Form of [sie]}•Hast du '''ihr''' das Buch gegeben?}•Did you give '''her''' the book?|Etymology 3}From Old High German ira.|Determiner}ihr:}#her qualifier:possessive}•Laura hat mir '''ihr''' neues Auto gezeigt.}•Laura showed me '''her''' new car.}•Die Katze spielt oft mit '''ihren''' Spielsachen.}•The cat often plays with '''her''' toys.}#its qualifier:when the owning object/article/thing/animal etc.,referred to,is feminine}•die Sonne und '''ihre''' Wärme}•the sun and '''its''' warmth|Etymology 4}From Old High German iro.|Determiner}ihr:}#their}•Die Kinder spielen mit '''ihrem''' Hund.}•The kids are playing with '''their''' dog.}•die Wolken und '''ihre''' Schönheit}•the clouds and '''their''' beauty

*in letzter Zeit*de{}|Alternative forms}die letzte Zeit|Adverb}#of late; lately; recently; referring to the recent past as a whole}#}in letzter Zeit Anton fragte ihren Bruder,ob sie beide '''in letzter Zeit''' gereist waren und wohin?}•Anton asked her brother whether the two of them had been travelling recently,and where to?|Usage notes}''In letzter Zeit'' is not freely interchangeable with other words meaning “lately,recently”,such as kürzlich,neulich,letztens,all of which refer to a particular time or event in the recent past,as in:''Ich habe sie kürzlich besucht.'' *inne-*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German - and from Old High German inne,adverbial form of in.}An alternative adverb (chiefly in Upper German) was from Middle High German īn,whence modern ein-. These then came to be distinguished in such a way that the short-vowel form expressed stationary location (adverb of+dative),while the long-vowel form expressed movement (adverb of+accusative). This distinction is largely maintained in modern German (cf. darin vs. hinein). Accordingly the prefix  is generally used with stationary verbs.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈɪnə/|Prefix}inne-:}#rare in,inside,interior}•{{prefixusex|de|haben|innehaben|t1to have|t2to hold,occupyAlt form of Alt form of}•{{prefixusex|de|halten|innehalten|t1to hold,stop|t2to wait,pauseAlt form of Alt form of}•{{prefixusex|de|wohnen|innewohnen|t1to dwell|t2to indwell,be inherentAlt form of Alt form of |Alternative forms}in- in nouns

*ist der Ruf erst ruiniert*de{}|Pronunciation}Ⓓ1/10/De-ist_der_Ruf_erst_ruiniert.ogg|Proverb}ist der Ruf erst ruiniert:}#ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt es sich ganz ungeniert
*ist der Ruf erst ruiniert, lebt es sich ganz ungeniert*de{}2017|Alternative forms}ist der Ruf erst ruiniert}ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt sich's völlig ungeniert;<ref name"Schemann">Hans Schemann:''Deutsche Idiomatik:Wörterbuch der deutschen Redewendungen im Kontext.'' 2nd edition with a complete reworked introduction,Walter de Gruyter,Berlin/Boston 2011,ISBN:978-3-11-021789-6,p. 675.</ref> ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt man völlig ungeniert|Etymology}lit:once the reputation is ruined,one can live it up completely unabashed. The phrase is attested,apparently for the first time,in w:Gustav Radbruch’s influential 1914 book ''Grundzüge der Rechtsphilosophie'' (see quotations below). Radbruch attributes it to w:Wilhelm Busch,but it has not been found in Busch’s writings.<ref name"citeweb">Jochen Schöpflin:''http://www.wilhelm-busch-seiten.de/werke/zitate2.html Wilhelm Busch:Angebliche Zitate,'' www.wilhelm-busch-seiten.de,February 9,2008; retrieved October 7,2015.</ref> So it was probably misattributed and may eventually be of popular origin. The 1914 attestation definitely disproves later attributions to writer w:Bertolt Brecht and cabaret artist w:langde. One or both of these may have contributed to popularising the phrase,however.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˌɪst dɛɐ̯ ˈʁuːf eːɐ̯st ʁuiˌniːɐ̯t ˌleːpt əs zɪç ɡant͡s ˈʊnʒeˌniːɐ̯t/}Ⓓe/ef/De-ist_der_Ruf_erst_ruiniert%2C_lebt_es_sich_ganz_ungeniert.ogg}ist der Ruf erst ru+i+niert,lebt es sich ganz un+ge+niert|Proverb}ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt es sich ganz ungeniert:}#jocular once your reputation has been ruined,you can worry less about social convention and live life more freely; ≈ if you've got the name,you might as well have the game}#}ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt es sich ganz ungeniert Gegenüber der Selbstherrlichkeit der Sitte gibt es nur den Trost Wilhelm Buschs:«'''Ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt man völlig ungeniert'''.» Nur dadurch unterscheidet sich also die Sitte vom Recht – und nur vom gegenwärtigen Recht –,daß sie die Strafe der Entziehung des Normenschutzes,die Friedlosigkeit noch kennt.}#}'''2013''' March 3rd,Simone Schmollack:''Ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,'' in ''taz.die tageszeitung,'' no. 10051,p. 4 (http://www.taz.de/!5071826/print archive; retrieved October 7,2015):}#}:Man kann machen,was man will,so nach dem Motto:'''Ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt es sich ganz ungeniert'''.+One can do what one wants to,as if to say:'''if you've got the name,you might as well have the game'''.}#more negative once their reputation is ruined,people tend to cast aside all decency}#}'''2006''' November 16th,''Wider die Leichenfledderei,'' in ''Lausitzer Rundschau'' (http://www.lr-online.de/regionen/spree-neisse/guben/Wider-die-Leichenfledderei;art1051,1442463 URL; retrieved October 7,2015):}#}:Ein Sturm der Entrüstung gegen derartige Leichenfledderei,angefangen vom Bürgermeister Klaus-Dieter Hübner und allen,denen das Ansehen unserer guten Stadt am Herzen liegt,sollte sich in Protestbriefen ausdrücken,denn „'''ist der Ruf erst ruiniert,lebt es sich ganz ungeniert'''.“+An outcry over such a vilification,first and foremost by the mayor Klaus-Dieter Hübner and by all those for which the good reputation of our fine town is dear to their hearts,should be expressed in form of protest letters because “'''if you've got the name,you might as well have the game'''”.

*Junge*de{}|Alternative forms}Jung|Etymology}Fixed nominalisation of from Middle High German young,from Old High German young.}Already occasionally in from German gmh,later gaining a fixed noun form based on its weak nominative inflection (giving ''ein Junge'' instead of ''ein'' Junger). The recognition as the normal standard term for “boy” is based on Central and Low German usage and has only fully asserted itself during the 20th century (compare Knabe). *Kadavergehorsam*de{}|Etymology}From Kadaver+Gehorsam,lit. "cadaverous obedience","corpse-obedience" or "corpse-like obedience" (Porter 2013).}Ultimately a rendition of an expression in the ''Constitutiones'' by Ignatius of Loyola (1558),'' qui sub Obedientia vivunt,se ferri ac regi a divina Providentia per Superiores suos sinere,(Latin) debent perinde,ac si cadaver,(Latin) essent ''. This expression was satirized by critics of the Jesuit order in Germany after 1814,in the German translation '''''wie wenn sie ein Cadaver wären'''''. The equivalent French expression as coined by Eugène Sue (1845) was ''obéissance de cadavre'' or ''obéissance cadavérique''.}The German compound appears in the 1870s,in the context of the 1872 prohibition of the Jesuit order in Germany.}The German term also entered usage as a loanword in other European languages,and by the 20th century it was applied more typically to the blind loyalty in Prussian militarism rather than in the Jesuit order.|Pronunciation}Ⓓ8/83/De-Kadavergehorsam.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#blind obedience,fanatical or excessive loyalty}#}'''1875''' (indirect speech attributed to Burghard Freiherr von Schorlemer-Alst (1825-1895) in a summary of a parliamentary debate of 7-10 May 1875),Wilhelm Müller,''Politische Geschichte der Gegenwart:IX Das Jahr 1875'' (1876),p. 49.}#}:Wozu denn das ewige Gerede von dem '''Kadavergehorsam''' in einer Zeit,in welcher der '''Kadavergehorsam''' gegen den Fürsten Bismarck einen bisher ungeahnten Grad der Ausbildung erreicht habe.

*kahl*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German kal (inflected from Middle High German kalwe),from Old High German kalo,from Old High German chalo,from Proto-Germanic tnaked,bald,from Proto-Indo-European naked,bald. The form  (instead of ) is based on the Middle High German uninflected stem. However,the lengthened vowel points to influence by varieties that reduce ''-lw-'' to ''-l-'' even in open syllables; these include from Middle Low German kāl (inflected from Middle Low German kāle). See the same development in fahl. Cognate with from Dutch kaal,from English callow,and further from Italian calvo,from Russian tnude,from Persian trkal,from Romanian chel.|Pronunciation}IPA:/kaːl/}Ⓓf/fb/De-kahl.ogg}Rhymes:aːl}Karl some speakers|Adjective}#bald,hairless}#figurative barren,bleak,empty,stark,bland|Usage notes}Now used chiefly in the figurative sense or of portions of the skin:. Of persons one more commonly says kahlköpfig or glatzköpfig (both literally "bald-headed"). Even more usual is the expression m:litto have a bald head.

*Kanzler*de{}|Alternative forms}Kantzler|Etymology}From Middle High German kanzelære,from Old High German canzilāri (ca. 900),borrowed from German cancellārius,derived from Latin cancellus. from German -er,but semantically pertaining more closely to Kanzlei (itself derived from the former). Compare from English chancellor.}The use for a head of government developed in a monarchic context from that for a senior administrator. After WWI it was maintained in the newly created republics,particularly as the respective heads of state (Präsident) continued to have far-reaching competences. At least in Germany this is no longer the case,making the title somewhat abstract.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈkant͡s.lɐ}Ⓓ7/79/De-Kanzler.ogg}Kanz+ler|Noun}(mask.)}#chancellor gloss:title of a head of government}#Germany short for [Bundeskanzler]}#historical short for [Reichskanzler]}#chancellor gloss:kind of secretary}#education head of the administration of a university}#diplomacy head of the administration of an embassy or consulate}#historical head of a chancellory; chief secretary of a bishop or ruler|Derived terms}Altbundeskanzler}Altkanzler}Antikanzler}Bundeskanzler}Bundesvizekanzler}Erzkanzler}Exkanzler}Gegenkanzler}Großkanzler}Neukanzler}Prokanzler}Reichserzkanzler}Reichskanzler}Reichsvizekanzler}Schattenkanzler}Schatzkanzler}Staatskanzler}Staatskanzler}Vizekanzler}Volkskanzler}Kanzleramt|Proper noun}m:f,s:-with an article,s:-,genitive:Kanzlerswith an article,plural:[Kanzlers])}#surname:de|Alternative forms}Kantzler

*Karnickel*de{}wikipedia:langde|Etymology}From earlier nds-de,from a variant of from Middle Low German kanīn,from Middle French connin (see Kaninchen). The form is probably based on from Latin cunīculus. The ''-r-''might have entered the word from the Brandenburg area,where non-rhotic and strongly rhotic Low German dialects neighboured. The sense “take away” may be partially influenced by etymology 2 below.|Verb}de-verb}#ambitransitive to collect (money),to demand and enregister (a payment),to act as cashier}•Wir '''kassieren''' die Beiträge vierteljährlich.}•We '''collect''' the fees quarterly.}•Sie hat verpackt,ich habe '''kassiert'''.}•She wrapped the wares,I was '''doing the cashier'''.}#ambitransitive to earn,cash in (money)}•Ich habe 250 Euro '''kassiert'''.}•I '''earned''' 250 euro.}•Die einen sterben im Krieg,die andern '''kassieren'''.}•There are those who die in a war and those who '''cash in'''.}#transitive to receive,get,earn}•Für ihr Debütalbum '''kassierte''' sie viel Lob.}•She '''got''' a lot of praise for her debut album.}#ambitransitive to receive,take in (something negative)}•Die Mannschaft '''kassierte''' viele Gegentore.}•The team '''received''' a lot of goals.}•Wenn du so weiter machst,'''kassierst''' du!}•If you keep on like this,you'll '''take''' a beating.}#transitive to take something away,to snatch,rake}•Die Lehrerin '''kassierte''' die Handys der Schüler.}•The teacher '''took away''' the pupils’ mobiles.|Derived terms}abkassieren}einkassieren}Kassierer|Etymology 2}From Middle High German kassieren (West Central German,14th c.),probably from Middle Dutch casseren (13th c.),from Old French casser,from Old French tto annul. *Kavalier*de{}|Etymology}Borrowed it,from Old French chevalier,from horse rider.}Early loans into Middle High German,as ''cavali(e)r'',are recorded for the 14th century,but remained without direct continuants.}Renewed loan in the later 16th century,as ''Caval(l)ier,Cavaglier,Cavalierer '',at the time with Italian plural ''Cavalieri'',but in the 17th century replaced with the French plural ''Cavaliers''. The word rises in popularity during the 17th century and becomes the equivalent of "gentleman",the term for the ideal of the educated,well-mannered member of the upper classes. The word is productive in compounds during the 17th and 18th centuries.|Pronunciation}IPA:/kavaˈliːɐ̯/standard}IPA:/ˈkavaˌliːɐ̯/variant,chiefly in the dated colloquial sense}Ⓓf/fe/De-Kavalier.ogg}Rhymes:iːɐ̯|Noun}(mask.)}#slightly gentleman}#dated boyfriend; sweetheart of a girl|Usage notes}Nowadays the more common,more general,and more positive word is Gentleman. ''Kavalier'' has become restricted to polite behaviour towards women and may have an overtone of flattery or ingratiation,rather than tact and grace.|Synonyms}Gentleman}Ritter|Derived terms}Kavaliersdelikt}Kavaliersschmerzen

The word is a member of a Wortsippe which also includes Keil,Cognate German tball,sphere and Kiel.}No cognates of  are known outside of German (other than loans from German in Dutch,Scandinavian as well as Baltic and Slavic languages). from French quille seems to be a reflex of an Old Frankish form of the word. from Proto-Slavic tstick,staff,rod has diverse proposed origins.}The German word Keil is closely related,compared by Grimm to the relationship of from Latin twedge with from Latin tcone. *kein Blatt vor den Mund nehmen*de{}|Etymology}not to take a leaf/sheet in front of one’s mouth. Compare the same in from Dutch geen blad voor de mond nemen. Further origin uncertain. Sometimes claimed to derive from a custom among stage actors,who apparently used tree leaves or sheets of paper as a kind of mask. Also said to be from the use of a sheet of paper to muffle one’s voice when speaking privately in company. *-keit*de{}|Etymology}Result of an etymologically wrong segmentation (rebracketing) of two suffixes in Upper German dialects of Middle High German:from Middle High German -ec (modern -ig) and -heit:''-ec-heit'' was interpreted as ''-e-keit''. Later this phenomenon spread to other suffixes,and even to Central German dialects,in which the equivalents of ''-ig'' had never been pronounced with a final k-sound. (Compare the modern standard pronunciation of -ig -ɪç.) However,in some northern dialects of Central German,like Ripuarian,from Central Franconian -keit is still absent or has only recently been introduced from standard German. Compare from Saterland Frisian -igaid.|Pronunciation}IPA:aaGermany}IPA:aaAustria}Ⓓ1/1f/LL-Q188_%28deu%29-Frank_C._M%C3%BCller--keit.wav|Suffix}(fem.)}#-heit}•wirksam|Usage notes}See -heit for notes on the use of the two variants.|Derived terms}suffixsee:de}

*kennen*de{}|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆ǵneh₃-}from Ingush tree1}From Middle High German kennen,from Old High German kennan,from Proto-West Germanic to know,from Proto-Germanic to know,a causative form of from Proto-Germanic ⋆kunnaną formed with the suffix from Proto-Germanic ⋆-janą. Cognate to from Bavarian kennan,from Dutch kennen,from Scots - and from Kenyang to know.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈkɛnən/}De-kennen.ogg(Germany)}De-kennen2.ogg(Germany)}De-at-kennen.ogg(Austria)|Verb}kennen(kannte,gekannt,kennte)}#transitive to know; to be acquainted with; to be familiar with}#}kennen Die Beseitigung des Schlendrians werde ich wohl nicht mehr erleben,auch dann nicht,wenn Plato selber aus der Asche auferstünde und die deutschen Schulmänner die richtige Aussprache lehrte. Sie würden ihm beweisen,daß er sich irre:er habe in den mehr als zwei Jahrtausenden seit seinem Tode gewiß die richtige Aussprache vergessen; sie aber,die deutschen Oberlehrer und Direktoren,'''kennten''' sie ganz genau:sie wäre buchstäblich so wie das Neuhochdeutsche des 20. Jahrhunderts gewesen.}•The abolition of this sloppy pronunciation of Ancient Greek I will probably never witness,not even should Plato himself rise from the ashes to teach to the German pedagogues the correct pronunciation. They would show him that he was mistaken:that he must have forgotten the correct pronunciation in the more than two millennia following his death,but that they,the German head teachers and principals,'''knew''' exactly what it was like:precisely the same as the New High German of the 20th century.|Usage notes}Although the senses of both ''kennen'' and wissen are covered by English “to know”,the two German verbs are only occasionally interchangeable. Only ''wissen'' is generally used with a following subclause (I know that...,how...,when...,etc.). With nouns the distinction may be more difficult.  is used with facts and memorized information (“to be aware of”,m+:savoir,m+:saber),whereas ''kennen'' is used with concepts,ideas,backgrounds (“to be familiar with”,m+:connaître,m+:conocer). Compare the following two sentences,both of which translate literally as “Do you know the street that he mentioned to us?”:

*Kerze*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German kerze,from Old High German kerza,from Old High German charza,from either from Latin covered with wax or from Latin charta (“sheet of papyrus”,in this case referring to layers of birch bark from which candles were made). The latter explanation is typically preferred,though the former is semantically more suggestive.
